images.title: Comparison of Targeted vs. General Medical Treatments
images.description: A vintage-style medical infographic comparing two treatments for women over 50 with a specific genetic marker. It highlights the superior effectiveness and lower side effects of targeted Treatment A versus the secondary Treatment B.
images.transcript: FILTER: WOMEN OVER 50 WITH GENETIC MARKER X. RANK 1: TREATMENT A. RANK 2: TREATMENT B. GENETIC MARKER X TARGETED. EFFECTIVENESS 92%. SIDE EFFECTS: LOW. OPTIMAL OUTCOME. EFFECTIVENESS 65%. SIDE EFFECTS: MODERATE. SECONDARY OPTION. SCIENTIFIC ILLUSTRATION DATABASE - VOLUME IV. WarOnDisease.org.
images.socialCaption: Personalized medicine is the key to better outcomes. By targeting specific genetic markers, we can increase effectiveness to 92% while minimizing side effects. #WarOnDisease #MedicalInnovation #Genetics
images.twitterText: The difference between 'generic' and 'targeted' medicine is life-changing. Targeted treatments offer 92% effectiveness for specific patient groups. This is why we need the 1% Treaty for research. #WarOnDisease #PrecisionMedicine
images.linkedInText: This illustration from the 'War on Disease' initiative demonstrates the power of precision medicine. By investing in research that identifies genetic markers, we move from 65% effectiveness to 92%, drastically improving patient quality of life.
images.speakerNotes: This slide illustrates the impact of personalized medicine. On the left, Treatment A targets a specific genetic marker, resulting in a 92% success rate. On the right, Treatment B represents a more traditional, broader approach which is significantly less effective and causes more systemic side effects.
talkingPoints: Targeted therapies significantly outperform generic treatments for specific demographics.
Genetic marker identification is the key to achieving a 92% effectiveness rate.
Investing in research reduces the burden of side effects on the patient.
The 'Optimal Outcome' is only possible through dedicated funding for medical innovation.
images.altText: A vintage-style medical comparison chart showing Treatment A (92% effective, low side effects) and Treatment B (65% effective, moderate side effects) for women over 50 with a specific genetic marker.
images.callToAction: Learn more at WarOnDisease.org
images.factCheckNotes: The data appears to be illustrative/conceptual to explain the benefit of personalized medicine rather than representing a specific real-world drug trial.

By shifting a small fraction of defense spending toward medical research, we could achieve orders-of-magnitude gains in global health efficiency and save lives at a fraction of current costs. #HealthcarePolicy #Innovation #GlobalHealth #EconomicEfficiency

Traditional high-cost interventions like cancer screening are compared against high-impact charities and systemic shifts.
The 1% Treaty represents a potential 50,300x improvement over malaria bed nets in terms of DALYs saved.

images.title: Redirecting Military Spending Towards Global Health Outcomes

images.transcript: Redirecting Competitive Incentives Towards Positive-Sum Health Outcomes. Military Contractors: Retain 99% of current budgets while redirecting 1% to fund global health security initiatives. 1% Treaty Fund ($27.2B). Pragmatic Trials (80%). Patients/Pharma: Patients: Subsidized trial access, reduced healthcare costs, faster innovation. Pharma: Reduced R&D Cost. Investor Returns (10%). Bond Holders: Investors: VICTORY Incentive Alignment Bonds offer 272% long-term returns through health savings and growth. Political Incentives (10%). Legislators: Politicians: ...gain reputation benefits, national security advantage, reduced defense pressure. Legislators: Political Support. Peace Dividend, Economic Growth & Stability. WarOnDisease.org
images.socialCaption: What if we redirected just 1% of global military spending to medical research? The 1% Treaty Fund could unlock $27.2B for innovation and global health security. #WarOnDisease #GlobalHealth #Innovation
images.twitterText: Just 1% of military budgets could generate $27.2B for medical research. See how the 1% Treaty creates a win-win for contractors, patients, and investors. 🩺🛡️ #GlobalHealth #1PercentTreaty #Innovation
images.linkedInText: The '1% Treaty' proposal demonstrates a positive-sum approach to global health. By redirecting a fraction of defense spending, we can drive down R&D costs, offer high-yield bonds for investors, and accelerate life-saving innovation. #HealthcareEconomics #PublicPolicy #Sustainability
images.speakerNotes: This diagram explains the mechanics of the 1% Treaty Fund. By shifting just 1% of military spending—allowing contractors to keep 99%—we create a $27.2 billion fund that fuels pragmatic trials, incentivizes bond holders with long-term returns, and provides political capital for legislators through a 'Peace Dividend'.
talkingPoints: Redirects $27.2B from military budgets to health without de-funding defense.
80% of funds go directly to pragmatic medical trials for faster innovation.
Creates 'VICTORY' bonds offering 272% long-term returns through health savings.
Generates a peace dividend that promotes long-term economic growth and stability.
images.altText: A circular flow chart in a vintage engraved style showing the 1% Treaty Fund. It illustrates how a $27.2 billion fund, sourced from 1% of military budgets, is distributed to pragmatic medical trials (80%), investor returns (10%), and political incentives (10%), creating a feedback loop of health and economic benefits involving military contractors, patients, pharma, bond holders, and legislators.

images.factCheckNotes: The $27.2B figure and the 272% return are based on specific economic modeling for the 1% Treaty initiative and may vary based on current defense budget fluctuations.

images.title: Current vs Proposed Drug Safety Monitoring Systems
images.description: An infographic comparing the slow, reactive nature of current voluntary drug safety reporting with a proposed automated Electronic Health Record (EHR) monitoring system. It uses the Vioxx case study to demonstrate how proactive surveillance could reduce detection time from years to months, potentially saving thousands of lives.
images.transcript: CURRENT SYSTEM (Vioxx Example); 5 YEARS OF VOLUNTARY REPORTING; YEAR 5; APPROVAL (Year 0); FAINT SIGNALS IGNORED; ADVERSE EVENTS UNDERREPORTED; Vioxx killed 38,000-55,000 people over 5 years... under the "safe" current system...; RECALL AFTER 38,000+ DEATHS; PROPOSED SYSTEM (Automated EHR Monitoring); LIVES SAVED GAP; MONTH 6; AUTOMATED EHR MONITORING; SIGNAL DETECTION; ALERT ISSUED; Proposed system uses automated EHR monitoring of all patients, detecting safety signals in months instead of years; SYSTEMIC CHANGE: Proactive surveillance replaces reactive reporting to prevent mass harm.; WarOnDisease.org
images.socialCaption: Our current drug safety system is dangerously reactive. By switching to automated EHR monitoring, we can identify risks in months rather than years, closing the 'lives saved gap' demonstrated by the Vioxx tragedy. #PatientSafety #HealthcareInnovation #WarOnDisease
images.twitterText: The Vioxx tragedy killed up to 55,000 people because safety signals were ignored for 5 years. Automated EHR monitoring could have detected these risks in 6 months. It's time for proactive surveillance. #DrugSafety #Healthcare #WarOnDisease
images.linkedInText: How do we prevent the next Vioxx? This infographic contrasts the 'Current System' of voluntary reporting with a 'Proposed System' of automated EHR monitoring. By shortening the detection window from 5 years to 6 months, we can save thousands of lives through proactive systemic change.
images.speakerNotes: This slide illustrates why our current pharmacovigilance system is broken, using Vioxx as a primary example. Currently, we rely on voluntary reporting which is slow and often ignores faint signals, leading to thousands of preventable deaths over several years. By moving to automated EHR monitoring, we can detect these same safety signals in just six months, closing the 'lives saved gap' through proactive surveillance.
talkingPoints: The current system relies on voluntary reporting, which often ignores early warning signs.
